Greek traditions disagree over whether Hera bore him alone or Zeus was his father.
His cult was particularly important at Athens and on Lemnos.

summary: The disabled master craftsman of Olympus, whose forge produces divine weapons, animated servants and works of impossible skill.
significance: The craftsman god, whose works in myth reflect the high status of skilled metalwork in Greek life.
myth: Greek traditions give Hephaestus different parents and two falls from Olympus. In one, Hera rejects her disabled child and throws him down; in another, Zeus casts him out for defending Hera. He lands on Lemnos and becomes the gods' smith. He makes palaces, thrones, armour and marvellous automata. In the *Iliad*, Thetis asks him to replace Achilles' lost armour, and his description of the new shield becomes an image of an entire human world.
earliestSource: Homer presents Hephaestus as both comic and formidable: his impaired gait draws divine laughter, while his technical power has no equal. Hesiod supplies alternative genealogical details.
religious: At Athens, Hephaestus was worshipped alongside Athena, linking skilled production with civic intelligence. The well-preserved temple commonly called the Hephaisteion overlooked an area associated with potters and metalworkers. Lemnos claimed a particularly close connection with the god.
historicalBackground: The god embodies the social ambiguity of craft: physically marginalised yet indispensable, working with dangerous fire and secret knowledge to create objects rulers and warriors cannot make themselves. Modern efforts to diagnose a medical condition from myth remain speculative.
archaeology: The Athenian Hephaisteion, inscriptions and vase paintings attest cult and iconography. Excavated workshops illuminate real Greek metallurgy but cannot identify a historical smith behind the deity.
laterInterpretation: Romans identified him with Vulcan. His self-moving tripods and golden attendants are now frequently discussed as ancient imaginings of robots, though they belong to poetic wonder rather than evidence for historical automation.

name: Perseus

claims.text: Perseus is the legendary son of Zeus and Danae and slayer of Medusa.
The story is already represented in Archaic Greek art.
Argive and Mycenaean communities incorporated Perseus into local foundation genealogies.
No independent evidence establishes Perseus as a historical individual.

summary: The Argive hero who kills Medusa, rescues Andromeda and becomes the legendary founder of Mycenae.
significance: One of the oldest Greek heroes, legendary founder of Mycenae and slayer of Medusa.
myth: An oracle warns Acrisius that his daughter Danae's son will kill him. He confines her, but Zeus reaches her as a shower of gold and Perseus is born. Mother and child are cast into the sea and survive. Later Perseus is sent to bring back Medusa's head. Athena and Hermes equip him; he approaches the Gorgon by reflection, decapitates her and escapes. On his return he rescues Andromeda from a sea monster and eventually fulfils the oracle accidentally by killing Acrisius with a discus.
earliestSource: Hesiodic poetry and early lyric preserve fragments of the story, while vase painting shows Perseus and the Gorgons from the seventh century BC. The continuous narrative survives most fully in later mythographers.
religious: Perseus received heroic honours and belonged especially to Argive identity. Genealogies made him ancestor of Heracles and founder of Mycenae, connecting communities and ruling houses to the age of heroes.
historicalBackground: The myth combines folktale patterns—an exposed child, a fatal prophecy, magical helpers and an impossible quest—with local claims about real places. Those structures explain transmission better than attempts to recover a Bronze Age biography.
archaeology: Mycenae is a real Bronze Age centre, but no inscription or object connects its foundation to Perseus. Archaic images demonstrate that his story was established early; they do not demonstrate the events depicted.
laterInterpretation: The rescue of Andromeda became a major subject in Roman and European art. Modern retellings often make Medusa the centre of the story, examining violence and power from the monster's perspective.

name: Medusa

claims.text: Medusa is the only mortal member of the three Gorgon sisters in Hesiodic genealogy.
Perseus kills Medusa by avoiding her direct gaze.
Gorgoneion faces served an apotropaic protective function in Greek art.
The story that Athena transformed Medusa after an assault by Poseidon is best known from the Roman poet Ovid and is not the earliest Greek version.

summary: The mortal Gorgon whose face turns viewers to stone and whose severed head becomes a powerful protective emblem.
significance: A monster whose severed head became one of the most widespread protective images in Greek art.
myth: Medusa is one of three Gorgon sisters and the only one who can die. Perseus is ordered to obtain her head. Guided by Athena and Hermes, he uses a reflective surface to avoid looking directly at her and cuts off her head while she sleeps. Pegasus and Chrysaor spring from her severed neck, children conceived with Poseidon. Perseus uses the head as a weapon before giving it to Athena, who places it on her aegis.
earliestSource: Homer knows the terrifying Gorgon head, while Hesiod supplies Medusa's genealogy and death. Early Greek art shows a monstrous, frontal face with staring eyes, tusks and protruding tongue.
religious: The *gorgoneion* was not simply an illustration of a story. Its confrontational face appeared on shields, temples, vessels and clothing as an apotropaic sign intended to repel danger. Athena's use of the head made terror protective.
historicalBackground: Versions changed substantially. Early Greek Medusa is born a Gorgon; the influential transformation narrative—in which she is assaulted by Poseidon in Athena's temple and punished—comes from Ovid's Latin *Metamorphoses* many centuries later.
archaeology: Gorgon images are abundant from the Archaic period onward and track changes from grotesque monster to beautiful woman with snakes. They establish the emblem's importance, not a zoological creature or historical encounter.
laterInterpretation: Medusa has become a symbol of female rage, trauma, protection and resistance. These readings are culturally powerful but should be identified as receptions of an ancient figure rather than presented as one original meaning.

name: Jason

claims.text: Jason leads the Argonauts' expedition to recover the Golden Fleece.
Medea's knowledge and magic enable Jason to complete Aeetes' trials.
The Argonaut story predates Apollonius' surviving Hellenistic epic.
No evidence establishes the voyage as a recoverable historical expedition.

summary: Leader of the Argonauts, whose quest for the Golden Fleece succeeds through Medea's aid and ends in betrayal at Corinth.
significance: The leader of the Argonauts, whose quest is one of the oldest Greek adventure stories.
myth: Jason's uncle Pelias has seized the throne of Iolcus. Ordered to fetch the Golden Fleece from distant Colchis, Jason gathers the Argonauts and sails in the Argo through a sequence of dangers. King Aeetes demands impossible tasks, but his daughter Medea falls in love with Jason and supplies the knowledge and drugs that make success possible. They flee together. Years later at Corinth, Jason abandons Medea for a royal marriage, provoking the catastrophe dramatised by Euripides.
earliestSource: Homer already refers to the Argo as famous, showing that some form of the voyage was familiar by the early Archaic period. Pindar gives an extended version, and Apollonius' third-century BC *Argonautica* is the fullest surviving epic narrative.
religious: Jason was woven into local genealogies and place traditions rather than worshipped through a single pan-Greek cult. Communities along imagined routes could attach landmarks, rites and founders to the voyage.
historicalBackground: The journey projects Greek navigation toward the Black Sea into heroic time. It may reflect later familiarity with eastern trade and colonisation, but the poem's geography and magical trials do not preserve a usable log of one Bronze Age voyage.
archaeology: Archaeology demonstrates Bronze Age and later contact across the Aegean and Black Sea. It cannot identify the Argo, Golden Fleece or crew. Proposed technical explanations for the fleece remain speculative.
laterInterpretation: Jason's reputation varies with the source. Adventure traditions centre his leadership, while Euripides exposes his opportunism and makes Medea's sacrifice and abandonment impossible to ignore.

name: Medea

claims.text: Medea is a Colchian princess whose aid enables Jason to obtain the Golden Fleece.
Euripides' Medea kills her children after Jason abandons her at Corinth.
Earlier traditions did not all assign the children's killing to Medea herself.
Medea's story repeatedly explores the status of the foreign woman within Greek communities.

summary: Colchian princess, healer and sorceress who secures Jason's quest, abandons her home and is later betrayed at Corinth.
significance: One of the most powerful and disturbing women in Greek myth, the subject of Euripides' great tragedy.
myth: Medea is daughter of Aeetes, king of Colchis, and descendant of the Sun. She helps Jason yoke fire-breathing bulls, defeat earthborn warriors and overcome the serpent guarding the Golden Fleece. She flees with him and uses dangerous knowledge to protect their escape. At Corinth Jason leaves her to marry a princess. In Euripides' tragedy, Medea kills the bride and king with poisoned gifts, then kills her own children and escapes in a chariot of the Sun.
earliestSource: Early epic fragments and lyric knew Medea, but surviving versions are uneven. Euripides' *Medea* of 431 BC and Apollonius' Hellenistic *Argonautica* are decisive, very different portraits: an abandoned adult exile and a young woman experiencing first love.
religious: Corinthian traditions connected Medea and her children with local rites. The evidence is complicated by later attempts to explain ritual through narrative and narrative through ritual.
historicalBackground: Medea is marked as foreign, female and intellectually powerful. Greek texts use her to test boundaries between insider and outsider, civilisation and barbarism, healing and poison, justified anger and intolerable violence.
archaeology: Vase paintings document changing scenes and emphases, including Medea rejuvenating a ram and escaping after the murders. Images show the tradition's development but cannot establish a historical woman.
laterInterpretation: Modern theatre repeatedly returns to Medea through questions of migration, race, motherhood, abuse and revenge. The child-killing version is dominant because of Euripides, not because Greek tradition was ever uniform.

name: Atalanta

claims.text: Atalanta is an exceptional hunter and runner raised outside conventional female domestic life.
She participates in the Calydonian boar hunt in the dominant surviving tradition.
Ancient sources preserve incompatible Arcadian and Boeotian genealogies for Atalanta.
Some traditions include Atalanta among the Argonauts while others explicitly exclude her.

summary: A formidable hunter and runner whose competing traditions resist any single fixed biography or genealogy.
significance: A heroine who outran and outhunted men, challenging the usual roles of women in Greek myth.
myth: Exposed as an infant and nursed by a bear, Atalanta grows into a hunter devoted to Artemis. She draws first blood in the Calydonian boar hunt, and Meleager awards her the hide, provoking a lethal quarrel with his relatives. In another famous story she agrees to marry only a man who can defeat her in a footrace; Hippomenes wins by distracting her with golden apples supplied by Aphrodite. Later the couple are transformed into lions.
earliestSource: Hesiodic fragments, lyric poetry and visual art preserve early elements. Later handbooks combine traditions that do not fit neatly together, including different fathers, regions and partners.
religious: Atalanta's closeness to Artemis places her in wilderness, hunting and resistance to marriage. Her eventual marriage and transformation make the story one of the many myths negotiating a girl's movement into adult social roles.
historicalBackground: It is misleading to force the Arcadian huntress, Boeotian runner and possible Argonaut into a single consistent life. Mythic figures could be shared, relocated and recombined as stories travelled.
archaeology: Greek vase painting and relief sculpture show Atalanta wrestling, hunting and racing. These images demonstrate her popularity and the range of episodes attached to her, not a historical athlete.
laterInterpretation: Atalanta has become a durable figure of female athletic independence. Modern versions often omit the coercive stakes of the marriage race or reinterpret her transformation as punishment for lost autonomy.

name: Prometheus

claims.text: Hesiod makes Prometheus responsible for the sacrificial division between gods and humans.
Prometheus steals fire for humanity after Zeus withholds it.
Zeus punishes Prometheus by binding him and sending an eagle to consume his regenerating liver.
Later traditions expand Prometheus from trickster into creator and champion of humanity.

summary: The Titan trickster who negotiates sacrifice, steals fire for mortals and endures Zeus' punishment for crossing divine boundaries.
significance: The Titan who gave fire to humanity, a lasting symbol of defiance and of the price of knowledge.
myth: At Mecone, Prometheus divides an ox into an attractive pile of bones concealed in fat and an unappealing pile of edible meat. Zeus chooses the deceptive portion, establishing why humans eat sacrificial meat while smoke and bones go to the gods. Zeus hides fire; Prometheus steals it in a fennel stalk. Zeus answers with Pandora for humanity and chains Prometheus while an eagle consumes his liver each day. Heracles eventually kills the eagle and releases him.
earliestSource: Hesiod's *Theogony* and *Works and Days* give the earliest surviving connected accounts. The later tragedy *Prometheus Bound* radically intensifies his role as a suffering benefactor who teaches humanity the arts of civilisation.
religious: Prometheus had cult associations especially at Athens, where a torch race connected him with fire and craft. His religious profile was narrower than his enormous literary afterlife.
historicalBackground: The story explains permanent conditions: sacrificial practice, the separation of humans and gods, labour, fire and technical knowledge. It is not a memory of one inventor discovering combustion.
archaeology: Attic art shows his punishment and release. Evidence for ritual confirms worship but cannot turn the Titan into a historical culture-bringer.
laterInterpretation: Prometheus became an emblem of intellectual rebellion, scientific ambition and resistance to tyranny. Mary Shelley's subtitle for *Frankenstein*, “The Modern Prometheus,” captures both creative power and catastrophic responsibility.

name: Pandora

claims.text: Hesiod presents Pandora as Zeus' response to Prometheus' theft of fire.
The gods furnish Pandora with beauty, craft, persuasion and deception.
In Works and Days Pandora opens a storage jar, not the small box familiar from later retellings.
Hope remains inside the jar, but Hesiod does not explain unambiguously whether this is preservation or deprivation.

summary: The first woman in Hesiod's account, fashioned by the gods as Zeus' dangerous answer to Prometheus and human fire.
significance: The first woman in Greek myth, whose jar released the troubles of human life — Hesiod's explanation of evil in the world.
myth: After Prometheus steals fire, Zeus orders Hephaestus to form a woman from earth and water. Athena teaches her weaving, Aphrodite gives desire, Hermes supplies a deceptive mind and the gods adorn her irresistibly. She is sent to Prometheus' brother Epimetheus, who accepts her despite a warning never to receive Zeus' gifts. Pandora opens a great storage jar and releases suffering, disease and toil into human life; only Hope remains within.
earliestSource: Hesiod tells related but not identical versions in the *Theogony* and *Works and Days*. The latter names her Pandora and narrates the jar.
religious: Pandora is principally a literary and explanatory figure, not the centre of a major cult. Her name, “all-gifted” or “all-giving,” also intersects with titles for earth divinities, complicating any simple origin story.
historicalBackground: The myth encodes an aggressively male account of marriage, labour and sexual reproduction: women are presented as both necessary and costly. Reading that ideology critically is essential; repeating it as a neutral Greek belief is not.
archaeology: Classical sculpture and vase painting sometimes show Pandora's creation. The evidence illustrates reception of Hesiodic themes rather than an archaeological event.
laterInterpretation: The “box” results from a Renaissance mistranslation or substitution for Hesiod's large *pithos* jar. Debate continues over Hope: is it retained for human use, or withheld as one more harm?

name: Cerberus

claims.text: Cerberus guards the entrance to Hades and prevents the dead from leaving.
Hesiod describes Cerberus with fifty heads, while later art and literature usually settle on three.
Capturing Cerberus alive is the final labour in the canonical set of Heracles' twelve labours.
No ancient source provides one completely consistent physical description.

summary: The many-headed hound guarding the underworld, subdued and brought to daylight in Heracles' final labour.
significance: The guardian of the underworld, whose capture was Heracles' final and hardest labour.
myth: Cerberus stands at the threshold of Hades, admitting the dead but preventing their escape. For his final labour Heracles must bring the hound to the upper world without weapons. With divine permission, he wrestles Cerberus into submission, displays him to Eurystheus and returns him below. Other visitors use different means: Orpheus charms the guardian with music, while Psyche later distracts him with drugged cakes in Roman narrative.
earliestSource: Hesiod calls Cerberus a fifty-headed, bronze-voiced dog born to Echidna and Typhon. Visual art and later literature increasingly give him three heads, a serpent tail and snakes rising from his body.
religious: Cerberus belongs mainly to poetic and visual representations of the underworld. Funerary beliefs did include guardians, thresholds and provisions for the dead, but there was no uniform Greek dogma about his exact appearance.
historicalBackground: The monster makes death's one-way boundary visible. Heroes who pass him demonstrate exceptional temporary access to a realm ordinary mortals enter only once.
archaeology: Vase paintings and sculptures show Heracles leading or wrestling Cerberus and document the development of the three-headed form. They are evidence for myth and iconography, not an underworld animal.
laterInterpretation: Cerberus became the standard name for an intimidating guard. Dante relocates him within Christian hell, while modern fiction and games retain the three-headed design more consistently than ancient sources did.

name: Ares

claims.text: Ares is named on Linear B tablets from Knossos.
In the Iliad Zeus calls Ares the most hateful of the gods to him.
Ares had relatively few major temples in Greece compared with other Olympians.

summary: The Olympian god of war in its violent, chaotic aspect — powerful, feared and little loved, even by the other gods.
significance: The god of the brute force of battle, set against Athena's strategy; his Roman counterpart Mars became one of Rome's greatest gods.
myth: Ares was the son of Zeus and Hera. In the *Iliad* he fights for the Trojans, and is wounded by the Greek hero Diomedes with Athena's help, bellowing like ten thousand men; Zeus tells him he is the most hateful of all the gods. In the *Odyssey* the bard Demodocus sings of his affair with Aphrodite, wife of Hephaestus, who traps the lovers in an invisible net for the gods to laugh at. His children with Aphrodite included Phobos (Fear) and Deimos (Terror), who rode with him into battle.
earliestSource: His name, *a-re*, appears on Linear B tablets from Knossos, possibly as a title of war. Homer gives the fullest early portrait.
religious: Ares had fewer major cults than most Olympians. He was worshipped at Sparta and in Thrace, which Greeks saw as his homeland, and had a temple in the Athenian Agora. The Areopagus, the "hill of Ares", where Athens' ancient council met, bore his name.
laterInterpretation: The Romans identified him with Mars, a far more honoured god, father of Romulus and patron of the Roman army. The planet Mars and the month of March are named after him.

name: Pan

claims.text: Pan was an Arcadian god of shepherds, shown with the legs and horns of a goat.
Herodotus says the Athenians founded a cult of Pan after he appeared to Pheidippides before Marathon.
The word "panic" derives from the sudden fear Pan was believed to cause.

summary: The goat-legged god of shepherds, flocks and wild places from Arcadia, whose sudden terrors gave us the word "panic".
significance: The god of the untamed countryside and its music, whose cult Athens adopted after Marathon and who became a lasting symbol of nature.
myth: Pan was usually said to be the son of Hermes. He had the horns, legs and beard of a goat, and roamed the mountains of Arcadia with the nymphs, playing the pipes. In one story he pursued the nymph Syrinx, who was turned into reeds to escape him; from the reeds he made the shepherd's pipe, the *syrinx* or panpipes. He was said to fill herds and armies with sudden, irrational fear — panic.
earliestSource: The Homeric *Hymn to Pan* tells of his birth and his delight in the woods. Herodotus records his appearance to the runner Pheidippides before Marathon.
religious: Pan was worshipped mainly in Arcadia, often in caves. After Marathon in 490 BC, Herodotus says, the Athenians gave him a cave shrine on the slope of the Acropolis, believing he had promised to help them; caves sacred to him and the nymphs were found across Attica.
laterInterpretation: Plutarch tells a famous story of a voice announcing "Great Pan is dead", later read by Christians as the end of paganism. Pan became a symbol of nature in Romantic poetry and art, and the Romans identified him with Faunus.

name: Eros

claims.text: In Hesiod's Theogony, Eros is one of the first beings to emerge after Chaos.
Later tradition made Eros the son of Aphrodite, a winged youth or child with a bow.
Plato's Symposium presents speeches in praise of Eros.

summary: The god of love and desire — in early myth a primal force of creation, later the winged son of Aphrodite with his arrows.
significance: Desire personified, central to Greek poetry and philosophy, and the origin of the image of Cupid.
myth: In Hesiod's *Theogony*, Eros is one of the first beings to appear, after Chaos and Gaia: "fairest of the immortal gods", who loosens the limbs and overpowers the mind of gods and men. He is a cosmic force that brings things together and makes generation possible. In later stories he becomes the son of Aphrodite, usually by Ares, a beautiful winged youth or mischievous child whose arrows make gods and mortals fall in love. Apuleius' Roman tale tells of his love for the mortal Psyche.
earliestSource: Hesiod's *Theogony* (c. 700 BC). Lyric poets such as Sappho, who called him "bittersweet", made Eros a central figure of love poetry.
religious: Eros had a cult at Thespiae in Boeotia, where a Praxiteles statue of him stood, and was honoured with Aphrodite at many sanctuaries and in gymnasia.
laterInterpretation: Plato's *Symposium* develops Eros into a philosophical force leading the soul towards beauty and truth. The Romans called him Cupid or Amor, and his image as a winged child with a bow passed into Renaissance and modern art.

name: The Muses
domain: Poetry, music, history and the arts

claims.text: Hesiod names nine Muses, daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne (Memory).
Homer begins both the Iliad and the Odyssey by invoking the Muse.
The word "museum" comes from the Museum (shrine of the Muses) at Alexandria.

summary: The nine goddesses of poetry, music and knowledge, daughters of Zeus and Memory, invoked by poets for inspiration.
significance: The source of inspiration in Greek thought — and of the words music and museum.
myth: The Muses were daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, the goddess of Memory, born in Pieria near Mount Olympus. They sang for the gods at their feasts, led by Apollo, and lived on Mount Helicon in Boeotia and on Parnassus. In Hesiod's *Theogony* they appear to him as he tends sheep on Helicon and give him the gift of song. Later tradition assigned each a field: Calliope (epic), Clio (history), Euterpe (music), Erato (love poetry), Melpomene (tragedy), Polyhymnia (hymns), Terpsichore (dance), Thalia (comedy) and Urania (astronomy).
earliestSource: Homer invokes the Muse at the start of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*; Hesiod first names all nine.
religious: The Muses had sanctuaries on Helicon and elsewhere, and schools and philosophers honoured them: Plato's Academy had a shrine to them. The Ptolemies' Museum at Alexandria was literally their "shrine".
laterInterpretation: Poets from Virgil to Milton invoked the Muse. Their name lives on in "music", "museum" and "amuse".

name: Hector

claims.text: Hector, son of King Priam, is the chief defender of Troy in the Iliad.
His farewell to his wife Andromache and son Astyanax in Iliad Book 6 is one of the poem's most famous scenes.
Hector was a historical individual.

summary: The greatest warrior of Troy, son of King Priam, who died at the hands of Achilles defending his city.
significance: The most sympathetic hero of the Iliad — a family man fighting for his home — whose death and burial frame its ending.
myth: Hector was the eldest son of Priam and Hecuba, king and queen of Troy, and the leader of the Trojan army. In the *Iliad* he drives the Greeks back to their ships while Achilles refuses to fight, and kills Patroclus, Achilles' friend, who has gone into battle wearing Achilles' armour. In Book 6 he says farewell to his wife Andromache and baby son Astyanax, who is frightened by the crest of his helmet; Hector takes it off and laughs. When Achilles returns, Hector faces him alone outside the walls, flees three times around the city, and is killed. Achilles drags his body behind his chariot, until Priam comes by night to ransom it. The *Iliad* ends with Hector's funeral.
earliestSource: Homer's *Iliad*, where he is the main Trojan hero.
historicalBackground: No historical Hector is known. Like other heroes of the Trojan War, he belongs to legend shaped by centuries of oral poetry.
laterInterpretation: Hector became a model of the noble warrior and patriot. In the Middle Ages he was counted among the Nine Worthies, and his farewell to Andromache was a favourite subject of painters.

name: Priam

claims.text: Priam is the king of Troy during the Trojan War in Greek legend.
In Iliad Book 24 Priam goes to Achilles' tent to ransom Hector's body.
The gold hoard Schliemann named "Priam's Treasure" is about a thousand years older than any Trojan War.

summary: The aged king of Troy during the Trojan War, father of Hector and Paris, killed when the city fell.
significance: The image of a father and king in defeat, whose meeting with Achilles over Hector's body is the emotional climax of the Iliad.
myth: Priam was the king of Troy, set on the throne as a boy after Heracles sacked the city and killed his father Laomedon. He had fifty sons, among them Hector and Paris, and many daughters, including Cassandra. When Paris carried off Helen, Priam took her into his family and so brought the Greek army to Troy. In *Iliad* Book 24, after Achilles has killed Hector, Priam goes alone by night to the Greek camp, guided by Hermes, kisses the hands of the man who killed his son, and ransoms the body. Achilles, thinking of his own father, weeps with him. When Troy fell, Achilles' son Neoptolemus killed Priam at the altar of Zeus in his own palace.
earliestSource: Homer's *Iliad*; his death is told in the lost epics of the Trojan cycle and in Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 2.
archaeology: Heinrich Schliemann named a gold hoard found at Troy in 1873 "Priam's Treasure", but it dates to about 2400 BC, a thousand years before any plausible Trojan War.
laterInterpretation: His death at the altar became a symbol of the fall of a city and the cruelty of war, retold by Virgil and painted many times.

name: Penelope

claims.text: Penelope, wife of Odysseus, waits twenty years for his return in the Odyssey.
She delays the suitors by weaving and secretly unweaving a burial shroud for Laertes.
She tests the disguised Odysseus with the secret of their bed built around an olive tree.

summary: The wife of Odysseus, who kept faith and outwitted her suitors on Ithaca for twenty years until her husband returned.
significance: The Odyssey's match for Odysseus in cunning, and for later ages the model of the faithful and clever wife.
myth: Penelope was the wife of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, and mother of their son Telemachus. While Odysseus was away at Troy and on his wanderings, more than a hundred suitors gathered at their palace, feasting on its wealth and demanding that she choose one of them to marry. She said she would choose once she had woven a shroud for Odysseus' father, Laertes — and for three years she wove it by day and unpicked it by night, until a maid betrayed her. When Odysseus returned disguised as a beggar, she set the suitors the test of stringing his great bow, which only he could do. Even after the suitors were killed, she tested him herself, ordering their bed to be moved; only Odysseus knew it could not be, because he had built it around the trunk of a living olive tree.
earliestSource: Homer's *Odyssey*, where she is a central figure.
historicalBackground: Penelope belongs to legend; no historical figure lies behind her.
laterInterpretation: Penelope became the model of the faithful wife from antiquity onward. Modern writers, such as Margaret Atwood in *The Penelopiad*, have retold the story from her point of view.

name: Orestes and the House of Atreus

claims.text: In myth Orestes avenged his father Agamemnon by killing his mother Clytemnestra.
Aeschylus' Oresteia dramatises the curse on the House of Atreus and Orestes' trial at Athens.
The Spartans claimed to have recovered the bones of Orestes in the 6th century BC.

summary: The son of Agamemnon who avenged his father by killing his mother, the last act of the curse on the House of Atreus.
significance: The centre of Greek tragedy's greatest family saga, whose trial in Aeschylus' Oresteia stages the birth of justice by law.
myth: The House of Atreus, rulers of Mycenae, was cursed across generations. Tantalus served his son to the gods; Atreus murdered his brother Thyestes' children and fed them to him. Atreus' son Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to win a wind for the fleet to Troy. On his return, his wife Clytemnestra, with her lover Aegisthus, son of Thyestes, killed him in his bath. Their son Orestes, sent away as a child, came back years later with his friend Pylades, was recognised by his sister Electra, and on Apollo's command killed Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. Pursued by the Furies for shedding a mother's blood, he fled to Delphi and then Athens, where he was tried and acquitted by Athena's court.
earliestSource: The *Odyssey* holds up Orestes' revenge as a model for Telemachus. Aeschylus' *Oresteia* (458 BC), Sophocles' *Electra* and Euripides' *Electra* and *Orestes* dramatise it.
religious: Herodotus says the Spartans, told by Delphi to find Orestes' bones, found and brought them home from Tegea in the 6th century BC, claiming his heroic protection.
laterInterpretation: The story has been retold endlessly, from Eugene O'Neill's *Mourning Becomes Electra* to Sartre's *The Flies*, and gave psychology the "Electra complex".

name: Ariadne

claims.text: In myth Ariadne, daughter of King Minos, helped Theseus escape the labyrinth with a thread.
Theseus abandoned her on Naxos, where Dionysus found and married her.
The Iliad mentions a dancing floor made for Ariadne at Knossos by Daedalus.

summary: The Cretan princess who gave Theseus the thread to escape the labyrinth, was abandoned by him on Naxos and married the god Dionysus.
significance: The heroine of the labyrinth story, and an image of abandonment and rescue that has inspired art, poetry and opera.
myth: Ariadne was the daughter of King Minos of Crete and Pasiphae, and half-sister of the Minotaur. When the Athenian hero Theseus came to Crete among the young people sent as tribute to be fed to the Minotaur, Ariadne fell in love with him. On the advice of Daedalus she gave him a ball of thread, which he tied at the entrance of the labyrinth and unwound as he went in; after killing the Minotaur he followed it back out. Ariadne fled with him, but Theseus left her asleep on the island of Naxos. There the god Dionysus found her and made her his wife, setting her bridal crown among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis.
earliestSource: The *Iliad* mentions the dancing floor Daedalus made for her at Knossos; Hesiod and later writers tell her story.
religious: Ariadne was honoured on Naxos and elsewhere, sometimes as a goddess, perhaps reflecting an older Cretan or Aegean deity whose name meant "most holy".
laterInterpretation: The abandoned Ariadne was a favourite subject of Catullus, Ovid, Titian and Richard Strauss's opera *Ariadne auf Naxos*. "Ariadne's thread" means a way out of a complex problem.

name: Daedalus and Icarus

claims.text: In myth Daedalus built the labyrinth for King Minos of Crete.
Daedalus and his son Icarus escaped Crete on wings of feathers and wax; Icarus flew too near the sun and fell.
Greeks credited Daedalus with early statues and many inventions.

summary: The legendary Athenian craftsman who built the labyrinth of Crete and escaped on wings with his son Icarus, who flew too close to the sun.
significance: The Greek archetype of the inventor and artist, and in Icarus a lasting image of ambition that overreaches.
myth: Daedalus was an Athenian craftsman of unmatched skill, who fled to Crete after killing his talented nephew out of jealousy. There he worked for King Minos. He built the hollow wooden cow in which Queen Pasiphae mated with a bull, producing the Minotaur, and then the labyrinth to imprison it. When he helped Theseus escape — giving Ariadne the idea of the thread — Minos shut him and his son Icarus in the labyrinth. Daedalus made wings of feathers and wax for them both. He warned Icarus not to fly too low, near the sea, or too high, near the sun. But Icarus soared upward, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea that bears his name, the Icarian Sea. Daedalus reached Sicily, where King Cocalus protected him from the pursuing Minos.
earliestSource: The *Iliad* mentions a dancing floor he made for Ariadne. The full story is told by later writers, above all Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.
historicalBackground: Greeks credited Daedalus with the first lifelike statues and inventions such as the saw and glue. His name, meaning "skilfully made", suggests a personification of craft.
laterInterpretation: Icarus' fall, painted in the scene attributed to Bruegel, became a symbol of overreaching ambition; Daedalus of the inventor and artist.

name: Orpheus

claims.text: Orpheus was a legendary Thracian singer whose music could charm animals, trees and stones.
He went down to the underworld to bring back his wife Eurydice, but lost her by looking back.
Orphic religious poems and teachings were attributed to him.

summary: The legendary singer of Thrace, whose music charmed all nature and who went down to the underworld to bring back his wife Eurydice.
significance: The ideal of the poet-musician, and the legendary founder of Orphism, a religious movement concerned with the soul and the afterlife.
myth: Orpheus was a singer from Thrace, son of the Muse Calliope and, in some accounts, of Apollo, who gave him the lyre. His music was so beautiful that wild beasts followed him, trees moved and rocks were softened. He sailed with Jason's Argonauts and drowned out the Sirens' song with his own. When his wife Eurydice died of a snake bite, he went down to the underworld and sang so movingly that Hades and Persephone let her return — on condition that he did not look back at her until they reached daylight. At the last moment he turned, and she vanished. Orpheus later died at the hands of Thracian women, the Maenads, who tore him apart; his head floated, still singing, to Lesbos.
earliestSource: He is named by the poet Ibycus in the 6th century BC; the story of Eurydice is told fully by Virgil and Ovid.
religious: From the 6th century BC, poems attributed to Orpheus taught that the soul was immortal and could be purified. Gold leaves buried with the dead and the Derveni Papyrus preserve Orphic texts.
laterInterpretation: Orpheus has inspired operas from Monteverdi's *L'Orfeo* (1607) and Gluck to Offenbach, and countless poems and paintings.

name: The Amazons

claims.text: In Greek myth the Amazons were a nation of women warriors living on the edge of the known world.
Battles with Amazons were among the most popular subjects of Greek art.
Burials of armed women among the Scythians and Sarmatians may lie behind the legends.

summary: A legendary nation of women warriors from the edges of the Greek world, fought by heroes such as Heracles, Theseus and Achilles.
significance: A favourite subject of Greek art and myth, and perhaps a memory of real women warriors among the steppe peoples.
myth: The Amazons were a people of women warriors, said to live by the river Thermodon on the Black Sea or in the far north-east. They fought on horseback with bows, axes and spears, and in legend lived without men. Greek heroes repeatedly fought them. Heracles took the belt of their queen Hippolyta as one of his labours. Theseus carried off the Amazon Antiope, and the Amazons invaded Attica in revenge, a battle the Athenians later compared to the Persian invasion. Achilles killed the Amazon queen Penthesilea at Troy and, in some versions, fell in love with her as she died.
earliestSource: Homer mentions the Amazons in the *Iliad*; later poets and Herodotus told more.
archaeology: Battles of Greeks and Amazons (*Amazonomachies*) decorated the Parthenon, the temple at Bassae, the Mausoleum and countless vases. Archaeologists have found many graves of women buried with weapons among the Scythians and Sarmatians of the steppe, which may lie behind the legend.
laterInterpretation: The Amazons have stood for female strength and independence; the Amazon river was named after them by Spanish explorers.

name: The Titans
domain: The generation of gods before the Olympians

claims.text: In Hesiod's Theogony the Titans are the twelve children of Gaia and Uranus.
Zeus and the Olympians overthrew the Titans in a ten-year war, the Titanomachy.
The Greek succession myth has close parallels in Hittite and Babylonian myth.

summary: The older generation of gods, children of Earth and Sky, overthrown by Zeus and the Olympians.
significance: Central to the Greek story of how the present order of the gods came to be — and the origin of the word "titanic".
myth: In Hesiod's *Theogony*, the Titans were the twelve children of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky): six sons, including Oceanus, Hyperion, Iapetus and Kronos, and six daughters, including Rhea, Themis and Mnemosyne. Urged by Gaia, Kronos castrated Uranus and took power. Kronos swallowed his own children to stop them overthrowing him, but Rhea saved the youngest, Zeus. When Zeus grew up he freed his siblings and fought the Titans for ten years in the Titanomachy, with the help of the hundred-handed giants and the Cyclopes, who made his thunderbolt. The defeated Titans were imprisoned in Tartarus. Some, such as Themis and Mnemosyne, joined the new order; Atlas, son of Iapetus, was condemned to hold up the sky.
earliestSource: Hesiod's *Theogony* (c. 700 BC).
historicalBackground: The story of generations of gods overthrown by their sons closely resembles the Hittite *Song of Kumarbi* and the Babylonian *Enuma Elish*, evidence that Greek myth drew on Near Eastern traditions.
laterInterpretation: "Titanic" means enormous; the largest moon of Saturn is Titan, and the giant liner was named *Titanic*.

name: Serapis

claims.text: Serapis combined the Egyptian Osiris-Apis of Memphis with the appearance and powers of Greek gods such as Zeus, Hades and Asclepius.
Plutarch and Tacitus say that Ptolemy I brought his statue from Sinope after a dream; modern scholars doubt the story.
With Isis, his cult spread across the Hellenistic and Roman world.

summary: The god created under the early Ptolemies by blending the Egyptian Osiris-Apis with Greek gods, and worshipped across the Roman world.
significance: The clearest example of the fusion of Greek and Egyptian religion, and the patron god of Alexandria.
myth: Serapis had no myths of his own in the Greek sense; his stories were those of the gods he absorbed. As Osiris, he was the murdered and revived king of the dead, husband of Isis and father of Horus; as Zeus and Hades he was lord of the sky and the underworld; as Asclepius he healed the sick who slept in his temples. His cult statue showed him seated, bearded and mature, wearing a corn-measure (*kalathos*) on his head as a sign of fertility, with Cerberus at his feet.
earliestSource: The name comes from the Egyptian *Osor-Hapi*, Osiris-Apis, the dead Apis bull worshipped at Memphis, attested long before the Greeks. Serapis as a Greek-looking god appears in the reign of Ptolemy I. Plutarch and Tacitus tell how Ptolemy dreamed of a colossal statue and brought it from Sinope on the Black Sea, advised by the Egyptian priest Manetho and the Athenian Timotheus; the story is probably a later legend.
religious: His main temple was the Serapeum of Alexandria, with others at Memphis and Canopus, where the sick slept in the temple to receive healing dreams. He was the protector of the Ptolemaic dynasty and of sailors. Together with Isis, Harpocrates and Anubis, he was worshipped by Greeks and later Romans from Delos to Britain; the emperors Vespasian and Septimius Severus favoured him.
laterInterpretation: Older scholars saw Serapis as a political invention to unite Greeks and Egyptians; most now think the cult grew from the existing Memphite worship, adapted for Greeks rather than imposed. In practice Egyptians continued to worship Osiris and Apis, while Serapis became mainly a god of Greeks and Romans. His cult ended with the destruction of the Serapeum in AD 391.

name: Paris

claims.text: Paris, also called Alexandros, is a son of Priam and Hecuba of Troy.
In the Cypria he is the judge of a beauty contest between Hera, Athena and Aphrodite, and takes Helen as Aphrodite's reward.
In the Iliad Paris is a skilled archer and lover who avoids fighting, and is rebuked by Hector.
A Hittite text of the thirteenth century BC names a ruler Alaksandu of Wilusa, a possible echo of Alexandros of Ilios.

summary: The Trojan prince who judged the contest of three goddesses and carried off Helen of Sparta, setting off the Trojan War.
significance: The man whose choice and elopement brought about the destruction of Troy.
myth: Paris was born to Priam and Hecuba, but because of a prophecy that he would destroy Troy, he was exposed on Mount Ida and raised by shepherds. Zeus chose him to judge which of Hera, Athena and Aphrodite was the fairest. Each offered a bribe; he chose Aphrodite, who promised him Helen, wife of Menelaus. He sailed to Sparta and took her to Troy. During the war he fought mainly with the bow, and with Apollo's help killed Achilles. He was himself fatally wounded by an arrow of Philoctetes.
earliestSource: The Iliad shows Paris as handsome and cowardly, quarrelling with Hector and fighting a duel with Menelaus from which Aphrodite rescues him. The judgement and abduction belong to the lost Cypria.
religious: There was no significant cult of Paris. A Hittite letter from the thirteenth century BC mentions Alaksandu, king of Wilusa (probably Ilios), and some scholars link him with Alexandros.
laterInterpretation: The Judgement of Paris became a favourite subject for Greek vases and for painters from Cranach to Rubens, and it inspired Offenbach's operetta *La belle Hélène*.

name: Menelaus

claims.text: Menelaus was king of Sparta, younger brother of Agamemnon, and husband of Helen.
In the Odyssey Telemachus visits Menelaus' palace, where the king tells of his wanderings in Egypt.
The Menelaion, a sanctuary on a hill near Sparta, honoured Menelaus and Helen from the eighth century BC and incorporates a Bronze Age building.
Homer says Menelaus did not die but was sent to the Elysian Fields as the husband of Helen.

summary: The Spartan king whose wife Helen was taken by Paris, and who joined his brother Agamemnon in the war against Troy.
significance: The wronged husband whose cause drew the Greek kings to Troy.
myth: Menelaus, son of Atreus, married Helen and became king of Sparta. When Paris took her to Troy, he called on the oath of her former suitors and joined his brother Agamemnon in leading the expedition. In the Iliad he fights a duel with Paris, which he almost wins. After Troy fell he was driven off course for seven years, reaching Egypt, where Proteus told him how to get home. Once back in Sparta, he lived with Helen in wealth.
earliestSource: Menelaus appears throughout the Iliad as a brave but not outstanding fighter, and in Book 4 of the Odyssey as a prosperous host.
religious: At the Menelaion, on a ridge east of the Eurotas, worshippers made offerings to Menelaus and Helen from the eighth century BC, and Isocrates and Pausanias mention the cult. Excavations found a Late Bronze Age mansion beneath the shrine.
laterInterpretation: Euripides' *Andromache* and *Helen* show Menelaus as a petty, boastful figure, and *Orestes* makes him a self-serving relative; in the Odyssey he is a more dignified host.

name: Patroclus

claims.text: Patroclus is the closest companion of Achilles in the Iliad, from Opus in Locris.
In Book 16 he puts on Achilles' armour, drives the Trojans back, and is killed by Hector with the help of Apollo.
His death brings Achilles back into the fighting, and Book 23 describes his funeral games.
Homer does not describe the relationship as erotic, but Aeschylus and later authors did, and the question was debated in antiquity.

summary: The beloved companion of Achilles, whose death at Hector's hands brings Achilles back to battle.
significance: The hinge of the Iliad: his death turns Achilles' anger from the Greeks to Hector.
myth: Patroclus grew up in the house of Achilles' father Peleus after killing a boy in a quarrel. At Troy he accompanied Achilles. When Achilles withdrew from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon, Patroclus borrowed his armour to rally the Greeks. He drove the Trojans back, but was struck by Apollo, wounded by Euphorbus and killed by Hector, who stripped the armour. Achilles returned to avenge him, killed Hector and held funeral games in Patroclus' honour. His ashes were later placed with those of Achilles.
earliestSource: The Iliad, Books 9 to 23, is the main source. The Aethiopis and later epics treat his place in the cycle.
religious: Patroclus was honoured together with Achilles in hero cult around the Black Sea and at Troy, where travellers such as Alexander the Great laid wreaths at the tombs.
laterInterpretation: Aeschylus' lost *Myrmidons* made Patroclus and Achilles lovers, and Plato's *Symposium* discusses the idea. Madeline Miller's *The Song of Achilles* (2011) is a recent retelling.

name: Cassandra

claims.text: Cassandra was a daughter of Priam and Hecuba, mentioned in the Iliad as the most beautiful of his daughters.
Later tradition said Apollo gave her the gift of prophecy but, when she refused him, ensured that nobody would believe her.
After Troy fell, the Locrian Ajax dragged her from Athena's statue, and Agamemnon took her as a concubine.
In Aeschylus' Agamemnon she foresees her own murder and that of Agamemnon, and is killed by Clytemnestra.
She received cult in Italy and at Leuktra in Laconia, sometimes under the name Alexandra.

summary: The Trojan princess whose true prophecies were never believed, and who was taken captive by Agamemnon.
significance: The type of the truth-teller who is disregarded.
myth: Apollo, taken with Cassandra, gave her the gift of prophecy, but when she rejected him, he ensured that her prophecies would never be believed. She warned that Paris' voyage would end in disaster, and that the wooden horse hid enemy soldiers, but she was ignored. When Troy fell, the Locrian Ajax tore her from the statue of Athena, an act of impiety that angered the goddess. Agamemnon took her home as a captive, and Clytemnestra killed both of them at Mycenae.
earliestSource: The Iliad names Cassandra only briefly, as the first to see Priam bring Hector's body back to Troy. Her gift of prophecy and the curse are told in later sources such as Aeschylus and Apollodorus.
religious: A cult of Cassandra, under the name Alexandra, was observed in Laconia, and in southern Italy she was linked with the Locrian girls, sent annually to serve at Athena's temple in Ilion to atone for Ajax's crime.
laterInterpretation: Aeschylus' *Agamemnon* offers the best-known scene, in which she cries out visions at the palace door. 'Cassandra' now names a person whose warnings are ignored, and a 'Cassandra complex' in psychology.

name: Hecuba

claims.text: Hecuba was the wife of Priam, queen of Troy, and the mother of many children including Hector, Paris and Cassandra.
In the Iliad she offers a robe to Athena in a procession and begs Hector not to face Achilles.
After the fall of Troy she was allotted to Odysseus, and her daughter Polyxena was sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles.
In Euripides' Hecuba she blinds Polymestor, who killed her son Polydorus, and is turned into a dog.

summary: The queen of Troy, wife of Priam and mother of Hector and Paris, who lost her children and city and became a type of grief.
significance: The embodiment of the suffering of the defeated in Greek tragedy.
myth: Hecuba bore Priam many children. Before Paris' birth she dreamed she would give birth to a firebrand that would burn Troy. She saw her son Hector killed by Achilles, and Priam killed at the altar of Zeus, and her daughters carried off. After the sack she was given to Odysseus as a slave. In Thrace, on the way, she discovered that the king Polymestor had killed her youngest son Polydorus for his gold, and took her revenge, blinding him. She was said to have been transformed into a dog.
earliestSource: The Iliad shows her as the grieving mother, especially in Book 22 as she begs Hector to come inside the walls, and Book 24. Her later fate is told in the epic cycle and in Euripides.
religious: A headland on the Thracian Chersonese was called Cynossema, 'the dog's tomb', and sailors were said to see Hecuba's grave there.
laterInterpretation: Euripides wrote *Hecuba* and *The Trojan Women* about her. In Shakespeare's *Hamlet*, the player's speech on Hecuba prompts the question 'What's Hecuba to him?'.

name: Andromache

claims.text: Andromache was the wife of Hector, from Thebe in the Troad, and mother of the infant Astyanax.
The farewell between Hector, Andromache and their son in Iliad Book 6 is one of the best-known scenes in Greek poetry.
After the fall of Troy, the Greeks threw Astyanax from the walls and gave Andromache to Neoptolemus, son of Achilles.
The Molossian kings of Epirus claimed descent from Neoptolemus and Andromache.

summary: Hector's wife, who loses her husband, son and city at Troy and is taken as a slave to Greece.
significance: The type of the war widow in Greek literature.
myth: Andromache was the daughter of Eëtion, king of Thebe, whom Achilles killed along with her seven brothers. She married Hector, and bore Astyanax. When Hector went out to fight Achilles she begged him to stay on the walls. After his death, she watched Achilles drag his body behind his chariot. At the fall of Troy her son was killed and she was given to Neoptolemus, to whom she bore a son. In some versions she later married Helenus, a son of Priam, and ruled in Epirus.
earliestSource: The Iliad gives her scenes in Books 6, 22 and 24, with the most famous lament over Hector. Her fate after the war is told in the epic cycle and in Euripides.
religious: There was no extended cult of Andromache, but the kings of Epirus, including Pyrrhus, traced their descent from Neoptolemus and Andromache.
laterInterpretation: Euripides' *Andromache* and *Trojan Women* centre on her. Racine's *Andromaque* (1667) and Virgil's picture of her in Book 3 of the *Aeneid* made her a figure of sorrow and fidelity in later European literature.

name: Telemachus

claims.text: Telemachus is the son of Odysseus and Penelope, and a baby when his father left for Troy.
The first four books of the Odyssey, the Telemachy, follow his journey to Pylos and Sparta to seek news of his father.
Athena guides him, speaking in the form of Mentes and Mentor.
He joins his father in killing the suitors in Book 22.

summary: The son of Odysseus, who grows from a passive boy into a man while searching for his father and then fights beside him.
significance: The model of a son's passage to maturity in Greek epic.
myth: Telemachus grew up in the household overrun by his mother's suitors. Athena, disguised as an old friend of Odysseus, told him to call an assembly and sail to look for news. He travelled to Nestor at Pylos and Menelaus at Sparta, who told him his father was alive on Calypso's island. On his return he avoided an ambush by the suitors and found Odysseus at the swineherd's hut. Together they planned and carried out the slaughter of the suitors. Later traditions give him a marriage to Nestor's daughter Polycaste or to Circe.
earliestSource: The Odyssey is the earliest source, and the Telemachy in Books 1–4 shows his development. Lost epics such as the Telegony continued the story.
religious: There was no major cult. Ithaca's local hero worship focused on Odysseus himself.
laterInterpretation: Fénelon's *Les Aventures de Télémaque* (1699) was among the most read books of the eighteenth century. James Joyce used Telemachus for Stephen Dedalus in *Ulysses*.

name: Circe

claims.text: Circe is a goddess and enchantress who lives on the island of Aeaea, daughter of Helios and the Oceanid Perse.
She turns Odysseus' men into pigs with a drug, but Odysseus resists with the herb moly given by Hermes.
Odysseus stays with her for a year, and she advises him on the voyage to the underworld and on the Sirens, Scylla and the cattle of Helios.
Hesiod's Theogony names sons of Circe and Odysseus, and the Telegony makes Telegonus the son who later kills his father.

summary: The enchantress of Aeaea who turned Odysseus' crew into swine, then became his lover and adviser.
significance: The archetype of the sorceress who changes men's shape.
myth: Odysseus' ship landed at Aeaea. A party of men sent to explore the island found Circe's house surrounded by tame lions and wolves, were given a drugged drink and were changed into pigs. Hermes gave Odysseus the herb moly as a protection and told him to threaten her with his sword. She restored the men and welcomed them. After a year of feasting, she told Odysseus how to visit the underworld, avoid the Sirens and steer between Scylla and Charybdis.
earliestSource: Odyssey Book 10 is the earliest account, and Book 12 gives her warnings. Hesiod's *Theogony* gives her sons by Odysseus.
religious: The Romans identified Circe's island with Monte Circeo on the coast of Latium, where there was a cult place and local tradition of her residence.
laterInterpretation: Ovid, Spenser, Milton in *Comus*, and Joyce have all reworked the story. Madeline Miller's novel *Circe* (2018) retells the story from her view.

name: Calypso

claims.text: Calypso is a goddess or nymph on the island of Ogygia, who keeps Odysseus for seven years.
Her name means 'she who conceals', and Homer calls her the daughter of Atlas.
She offers him immortality if he stays, but he chooses to return to Penelope.
Zeus sends Hermes to order her to release Odysseus, after Athena speaks to him on behalf of the hero.
Ancient and modern writers have identified Ogygia with Malta or Gozo, but this is uncertain.

summary: The nymph of Ogygia who kept Odysseus on her island for seven years and offered him immortality.
significance: A figure who tests Odysseus' desire to go home against the offer of eternal ease.
myth: After the wreck of his last ship, Odysseus drifted for nine days to Ogygia, where Calypso took him in and made him her lover. She kept him seven years, though he spent his days weeping on the shore. When Athena complained to Zeus, he sent Hermes to order her to let him go. Calypso, resentful of the gods who permit goddesses no mortal lovers, obeyed. She helped him to build a raft, and gave him food and wind. Odysseus had refused her offer of immortality in preference for his wife.
earliestSource: Book 5 of the Odyssey gives the main account, and Odysseus retells it in Book 7. Hesiod makes her a daughter of Oceanus.
religious: There is no known cult of Calypso. Later writers placed Ogygia in the western Mediterranean, and Malta and Gozo claim it.
laterInterpretation: The story inspired Fénelon, Joyce and many poets. The name has been given to calypso music of Trinidad, and Calypso is also a moon of Saturn.

name: Polyphemus

claims.text: Polyphemus is a one-eyed giant of the Cyclopes and a son of Poseidon.
In the Odyssey he traps Odysseus and his men in a cave, eats several of them, and is blinded with a sharpened stake.
Odysseus tells him that his name is 'Nobody', so that when Polyphemus calls for help his neighbours do not come.
A seventh-century BC amphora from Eleusis shows the blinding, one of the earliest scenes from the Odyssey in art.
Later authors, including Theocritus, made him a lovesick shepherd who wooed the sea-nymph Galatea.

summary: The one-eyed Cyclops of the Odyssey whom Odysseus blinds and outwits by calling himself 'Nobody'.
significance: The best-known monster of Odysseus' wanderings, and the origin of Odysseus' feud with Poseidon.
myth: Polyphemus lived in a cave with his flocks. Odysseus and twelve men entered it to take supplies, and were sealed in by a boulder. The giant ate two men at a time. Odysseus offered him strong wine and told him his name was Nobody. When Polyphemus fell asleep, the men heated an olive stake and drove it into his single eye. His neighbours, hearing him shout that Nobody was hurting him, did nothing. The men escaped under the bellies of the sheep. As he sailed away, Odysseus boasted his true name, and Polyphemus prayed to his father Poseidon to curse him.
earliestSource: Odyssey Book 9. Folktale parallels of a blinded ogre are found in many cultures, and scholars have studied how Homer adapted such a tale.
religious: There was no cult. Ancient writers located the Cyclopes near Etna and around Sicily, and giant fossil bones found there were interpreted as their remains.
laterInterpretation: Euripides' satyr play *Cyclops* is the only complete example of its type. Theocritus and Ovid gave Polyphemus a lovelorn side, and the story has been often retold.

name: The Sirens

claims.text: The Sirens are creatures whose song lures sailors to their deaths, described in Book 12 of the Odyssey.
Odysseus has his crew plug their ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast so he can hear the song safely.
Greek artists show Sirens as birds with women's heads, and the figures often appear on tombs.
In the Argonautica the Argonauts survive because Orpheus drowns out the Sirens with his playing.

summary: The bird-women of the sea whose song lured sailors to destruction, and whom Odysseus heard by being tied to his mast.
significance: An image of fatal allure, and of knowledge that is deadly to possess.
myth: Circe warned Odysseus about the Sirens, who sat in a meadow beside a heap of bones and sang of the past. To pass them safely, he blocked his crew's ears with wax and had himself bound so that he could not steer towards the island however much he begged. The Sirens promised that he would know everything that happens on earth. According to later tradition, they were fated to die if a ship got past them, and they threw themselves into the sea.
earliestSource: The Odyssey, Book 12, in which the number of Sirens is two. Later sources vary, and give their parents as the river Achelous and a Muse.
religious: The Sirens appear as grave figures and mourners on funerary monuments from the sixth century BC, which suggests they were connected with lament and the afterlife.
laterInterpretation: Early depictions are of birds. Later artists made them part fish, which is the origin of the mermaid-like image. 'Siren' now also refers to an alarm sound.

name: Helios

claims.text: Helios is the sun god, son of the Titan Hyperion and Theia, who drives a chariot across the sky each day.
In Odyssey Book 12, Odysseus' men eat the cattle of Helios on Thrinacia, and Zeus destroys their ship with a thunderbolt.
Helios was the chief god of Rhodes, which held festivals in his honour and put his head on its coins.
The Colossus of Rhodes, built in about 280 BC, was a statue of Helios.
He was the father of Circe and of Phaethon, who tried to drive his chariot.

summary: The sun god, who sees and hears everything as he crosses the sky each day in his chariot.
significance: A god of the sun who was never one of the Olympians but who had an important cult at Rhodes.
myth: Helios rose each morning from the Ocean in the east, crossed the sky and sank in the west, returning by night in a golden cup. Because he sees everything, he informed Demeter that Hades had taken her daughter, and told Hephaestus of Aphrodite's adultery. His cattle grazed on the island of Thrinacia. When Odysseus' hungry men killed some, Helios threatened to shine among the dead, and Zeus smashed their ship. His son Phaethon, borrowing the chariot, lost control and was struck down by Zeus.
earliestSource: Homer and the *Homeric Hymn to Helios* name him as the sun. Hesiod gives his genealogy.
religious: The main cult was at Rhodes, where a four-horse chariot was thrown into the sea each year, and where the Colossus, built after the siege of 305–304 BC, represented him. From the Hellenistic period Helios was identified with Apollo and with Sol in Rome.
laterInterpretation: Roman emperors, including Aurelian, promoted Sol Invictus, and Helios appears as Christ in some mosaics of the third century AD.

name: Cadmus

claims.text: In myth, Cadmus was a Phoenician prince who founded Thebes in Boeotia and brought the alphabet to the Greeks.
He killed a dragon sacred to Ares and sowed its teeth, from which armed men, the Spartoi, grew.
Herodotus says that he saw inscriptions in 'Cadmean letters' at the temple of Apollo at Thebes.
The Greek alphabet was in reality adapted from a Phoenician script in the eighth century BC, in agreement with the tradition of a Phoenician origin.
Cadmus and his wife Harmonia ended their lives as serpents, living in the Elysian Fields or in Illyria.

summary: The legendary Phoenician founder of Thebes, who killed a dragon, sowed its teeth and was said to have brought the alphabet to Greece.
significance: The founder figure of Thebes whose Phoenician origin reflects the real debt of the Greek alphabet to Phoenicia.
myth: Cadmus was sent by his father, the king of Tyre or Sidon, to search for his sister Europa after Zeus carried her off. At Delphi the oracle told him to give up and follow a cow, and to found a city where it lay down. This was the site of Thebes. He killed the dragon guarding the spring of Ares, and Athena told him to sow its teeth. Armed men sprang up and fought until five survived, the ancestors of the Theban nobility. He married Harmonia, daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, and their children included Semele, mother of Dionysus.
earliestSource: The story is told by Pindar and Herodotus and filled out by later writers. Herodotus says the Phoenicians who came with Cadmus brought writing.
religious: Thebes' citadel was called the Cadmeia. Excavations there show a Mycenaean palace with Linear B tablets, although no archaeological evidence supports a historical Cadmus.
laterInterpretation: Euripides' *Bacchae* shows an aged Cadmus joining the Dionysiac revels. The transformation of Cadmus and Harmonia into serpents is told by Ovid.

name: Europa

claims.text: Europa was a Phoenician princess who, in myth, was carried to Crete by Zeus in the form of a bull.
She bore Zeus three sons: Minos, Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon.
The name Europe came into use for the continent, but the origin is disputed and may be Semitic or Greek.
Coins of Gortyn in Crete show Europa seated in a tree, and the island had a festival called the Hellotia, linked with her.

summary: The Phoenician princess abducted to Crete by Zeus in the form of a bull, who became the mother of King Minos and gave her name to Europe.
significance: The myth that links Phoenicia, Crete and the origin of the name of a continent.
myth: Europa, daughter of the king of Tyre or Sidon, was gathering flowers by the shore when Zeus appeared as a gentle white bull. She climbed on his back, and he swam with her across the sea to Crete, where he took his own form and fathered Minos, Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon. In Gortyn they were said to have lain under a plane tree, which never lost its leaves. Europa married the Cretan king Asterion, who raised her sons.
earliestSource: The *Iliad* mentions her as the mother of Minos and Rhadamanthys, with no details. The *Homeric Hymn to Apollo* uses 'Europe' for central Greece. Her abduction is told in Hesiodic poems, by Moschus and by Ovid.
religious: In Crete, a festival called the Hellotia honoured Europa as Hellotis, and her bones were said to be carried in a garland of myrtle. The bull recalls Minoan bull imagery.
laterInterpretation: Titian's *Rape of Europa* and Rembrandt's drawing made it a standard subject, and the myth is used for the name and imagery of the European Union, including the Greek 2-euro coin.

name: Bellerophon

claims.text: Bellerophon was a hero of Corinth (Ephyra) who tamed Pegasus and killed the Chimera.
In Iliad Book 6, Glaucus tells how King Proetus sent Bellerophon to Lycia with a sealed message demanding his death.
He also defeated the Solymi and the Amazons, and so won the daughter of the Lycian king Iobates.
Later accounts say he tried to fly Pegasus to Olympus and was thrown to earth.
Corinthian coins from the sixth century BC show Pegasus.

summary: The Corinthian hero who rode the winged horse Pegasus to slay the Chimera.
significance: The model of a monster-slaying hero, whose fall from the sky was a warning against presumption.
myth: Bellerophon fled from Corinth after killing a man and was purified by King Proetus at Tiryns. Proetus' wife Stheneboea falsely accused him of approaching her, and her husband sent him to Lycia with a letter asking for his death. King Iobates set him to kill the Chimera, thinking it would destroy him. With a golden bridle from Athena, Bellerophon caught Pegasus and killed the monster from the air. He later defeated Lycian enemies and married Iobates' daughter. Bold with success, he tried to ride to Olympus and was thrown, and lived the rest of his life as a wanderer.
earliestSource: The *Iliad*, Book 6, in the words of his grandson Glaucus. Pindar's *Olympian 13* tells of his taming of Pegasus.
religious: Bellerophon had a cult at Corinth, where he was honoured at a shrine outside the city and on the Craneion, according to Pausanias. In Lycia, tombs and reliefs show him.
laterInterpretation: Euripides wrote a lost *Bellerophon*. He and Pegasus were adopted in Corinthian art, and Pegasus is a symbol of poetic inspiration.

name: Pegasus

claims.text: Pegasus was a winged horse born from the blood of Medusa when Perseus cut off her head.
Hesiod makes him the offspring of Poseidon and Medusa.
Pegasus carried Bellerophon against the Chimera and later served Zeus by carrying his thunderbolts.
The spring Hippocrene on Mount Helicon was said to have been made when Pegasus struck the rock with his hoof.
Corinth used a Pegasus as its coin type from the sixth century BC.

summary: The winged horse born from the blood of Medusa, ridden by Bellerophon, whose hoof opened the spring of the Muses on Helicon.
significance: A symbol of poetic inspiration and the emblem of Corinth's coinage.
myth: When Perseus beheaded Medusa, Pegasus and his brother Chrysaor sprang from her neck. Poseidon was their father. Pegasus flew to Olympus and carried Zeus' thunder and lightning. He was caught by Bellerophon, using a bridle from Athena, and together they slew the Chimera. After Bellerophon fell, Pegasus carried on to Olympus. On Mount Helicon, he struck the rock with his hoof and the spring Hippocrene gushed forth, from which the Muses drank. In later legend he became a constellation.
earliestSource: Hesiod's *Theogony* gives his birth and name, deriving it from *pegai*, 'springs', where he was born near the Ocean.
religious: Pegasus had no worship of his own, but the Corinthians put him on their silver staters, called 'colts' by other Greeks, from the sixth century BC.
laterInterpretation: The Renaissance and later poets made Pegasus the steed of poets, and his name is used for a constellation and for many brands and projects.

name: The Chimera

claims.text: The Chimera was a fire-breathing hybrid with a lion's front, a goat's middle and a serpent's tail, according to the Iliad.
Bellerophon killed it with the help of Pegasus.
Hesiod makes it the offspring of Typhon and Echidna.
Natural gas flames burning on the mountainside at Yanartaş in Lycia have been proposed as the basis of the story.
An Etruscan bronze statue of the Chimera, found at Arezzo in 1553, is among the best-known surviving depictions.

summary: The fire-breathing monster of Lycia, part lion, part goat and part serpent, killed by Bellerophon from the back of Pegasus.
significance: The origin of the word 'chimera' for a hybrid creature or an unattainable fantasy.
myth: The Chimera was a monster, lion in front, serpent behind and goat in the middle, breathing flames. It was bred by Amisodarus, king of Caria, and ravaged Lycia. Iobates, the king of Lycia, sent Bellerophon to destroy it, expecting him to die. Bellerophon rode Pegasus above the creature and shot it from out of range, or, in some versions, thrust a lump of lead on his lance into its throat, which melted in the flames and killed it.
earliestSource: The *Iliad*, Book 6, is the first account, and Hesiod's *Theogony* gives its parents Typhon and Echidna.
religious: In Lycia, the burning vents on Mount Chimaera near modern Çıralı, known in antiquity for their eternal flames, were identified with the monster's home and the area had a shrine of Hephaestus.
laterInterpretation: The Chimera of Arezzo, an Etruscan bronze of about 400 BC, became an icon of Renaissance collecting. In modern language a chimera is a fanciful idea or, in biology, an organism with mixed tissues.

name: Sisyphus

claims.text: Sisyphus was the legendary founder and king of Ephyra, later Corinth, known as the cleverest and most deceitful of men.
In the Odyssey's underworld scene he is condemned to push a boulder up a hill, which rolls down again each time it reaches the top.
He is said to have cheated death twice, first by chaining Thanatos and then by persuading Persephone to let him return from Hades.
Some ancient traditions made Sisyphus the true father of Odysseus.

summary: The cunning king of Corinth condemned in the underworld to roll a boulder uphill for eternity.
significance: An image of futile, endless labour.
myth: Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, founded Corinth and grew rich by cunning. He revealed to the river god Asopus that Zeus had carried off his daughter Aegina, and Zeus sent Death to punish him. Sisyphus chained Death, so that no one could die until Ares freed him. He then tricked Hades again by ordering his wife to omit funeral rites, and talked Persephone into letting him go back to the world of the living. When he died of old age, he was condemned in Tartarus to push a great stone to the top of a hill, only to see it roll back.
earliestSource: The *Iliad* calls him the craftiest of men, and Odysseus sees his torment in the underworld in *Odyssey* Book 11.
religious: The Isthmian Games were said to have been founded by Sisyphus in honour of his dead nephew Melicertes. Pausanias reports that his tomb was shown on the Isthmus.
laterInterpretation: Albert Camus' essay *The Myth of Sisyphus* (1942) makes the figure a symbol of absurdity and defiance, concluding that one must imagine Sisyphus happy.
